ULA Rocket Turns 40 Amazon Internet Satellites to Bits When It Fails During Ascent
8 photos
Photo: Amazon Leo
It's been a sort of explosive weekend for the American space industry, as two high-profile missions, executed by SpaceX and the United Launch Alliance (ULA), ended with spectacular failures. But whereas the explosion of the SpaceX Super Heavy as it came back to the pad was offset by the Starship doing exactly that, thus saving Flight 15, ULA's new Vulcan rocket failed completely and took a customer payload with it.
On Sunday, November 15, Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida witnessed the liftoff of a ULA Vulcan rocket loaded with 40 broadband Internet satellites for Amazon's Leo constellation (previously known as Project Kuiper).
The launch went without any issues, and everything (including engine cutoff and second stage ignition) seemed on track for the rocket's cargo to take its place in the network that will ultimately comprise some 3,000 satellites. Then, just ten minutes or so into the flight, the Vulcan failed, taking the 40 bits of hardware with it.
The incident is too fresh for ULA to know exactly what happened, so we'll have to probably wait a bit to learn what went wrong. For the rocket maker, the outcome could have a number of implications for the relatively new design.
Vulcan Centaur by its full name, on account of it using a Centaur V second stage, the rocket was first launched at the beginning of 2024, when it carried the Astrobotic Peregrine lunar lander on behalf of NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program. Since then, it has flown three more times with no incident.
This weekend's launch was supposed to be the fifth, but also the first of no less than 38 Vulcan Amazon Leo missions. Before now, Amazon launched its satellites using the Atlas V, which flew to space eight times with this cargo on board.
Normally, the new Vulcan comes in four configurations, namely with zero, two, four, and six solid rocket boosters (SRBs). The version used this past weekend is the one with a low-Earth orbit-optimized configuration, the VC6L, which comprises six SRBs and a longer-length payload fairing.
The Vulcan first stage is 17.7 feet (5.4 meters) in diameter and stands 109.2 feet (33.3 meters) tall. It carries tanks to hold the liquefied natural gas (LNG) and methane fuel, and is equipped with a couple of BE-4 engines sourced from Blue Origin.
Each of the powerplants has a rating of 550,000 pounds of thrust at sea level, and is backed by six graphite epoxy motor (GEM) 63XL solid rocket boosters that deliver, each, 459,600 pounds of thrust.
The Centaur V second stage, on the other hand, has the same diameter (duh!), but is much shorter, at 35 feet (10.7 meters). It too carries fuel tanks, filled with liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, which is sent to the two RL10C-1-1A engines strapped to it, each capable of developing 23,825 pounds of thrust. On its nose sits the payload fairing that comes in at 70 feet (21.3 meters) in this configuration.
When the Vulcan Centaur was announced, it was seen as a replacement for the Atlas 5 and Delta 4 families of rockets, and that continues to be so despite this recent failure. It's not clear at this point when the rocket will fly again, as that depends on the findings of the investigation into this weekend's mishap. We'll keep an eye on things and report back once we know more. Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today. ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard. We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible. ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available. — ULA (@ulalaunch) November 15, 2026
